Array_Indexing_Needs_Parentheses.short_definition: Learners believe that accessing an array element in Processing requires extra parentheses around the index expression, e.g. numbers[(i)] instead of numbers[i].
Array_Indexing_Needs_Parentheses.why_incorrect: While numbers[(0)] is syntactically valid, the parentheses inside the square brackets are unnecessary. The parentheses add no functional value unless the index expression involves multiple operations and needs to be grouped for precedence, e.g. numbers[(i + 1) * 2].
indicators: Array access uses parentheses directly inside brackets: something[(index)]
The parentheses contain only a literal or a simple variable
There is no operator precedence reason for the parentheses
when_not_a_misconception: Parentheses are used because the index expression involves arithmetic, e.g. values[(i + 1) * 2]

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Unnecessary parentheses around a simple literal index
Unnecessary parentheses around a variable index

examples_not_presenet.explanation: Parentheses are necessary due to operator precedence

Array_Length_as_Number.short_definition: Learners believe that the length of an array an only be accessed using a fixed number, rather than using the .length property. This leads to code that only works correctly as long as the array has exactly the hardcoded length, and breaks otherwise.
Array_Length_as_Number.why_incorrect: Hardcoding array lengths makes the code fragile and less flexible. If the array changes in size (e.g. because of different initialization or because it’s replaced), the loop may no longer behave correctly and may throw runtime errors such as ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. The correct way to access all elements of an array is the use of the built-in .length property, which always reflects the actual size of the array.
indicators: Array length is accessed using a fixed number in loops or conditions
No use of the .length property on the array
when_not_a_misconception: The fixed number is used for a specific purpose unrelated to the array's length, e.g. accessing a specific index
A variable representing the length is used

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Using a fixed number (10) instead of data.length in the head of the loop
Using a fixed number (10) instead of foo.length or foo2.length in the loop body

examples_not_present.explanation: Correctly using data.length to access all elements of the array
Correctly using foo.length to fill foo2 based on the actual length of foo

Array_Length_Only_in_Loops.short_definition: Learners believe that the .length property of an array can only be used inside loop conditions (typically in for loops). They might not realize that .length is a general property of arrays and can be used in any part of the code.
Array_Length_Only_in_Loops.why_incorrect: .length is a public property of every array in Processing and can be used anywhere in the code where the array’s length is needed, not just in loops.
indicators: Avoiding .length outside of a loop conditions and hardcoding its value
when_not_a_misconception: .length is used outside of loop conditions

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Fixed number (5) is used instead of .length when wanting to fill array2 with decreasing values, while .length is correctly used in the loop condition

examples_misconception_presenet.code:
int[] arrayToCopy = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int[] copy = new int[5];
examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Fixed number (5) is used instead of arrayToCopy.length when initializing the copy array

examples_not_presenet.explanation: .length is used both in the loop condition and in the assignment to array2

examples_not_presenet.code:
int[] arrayToCopy = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int[] copy = new int[arrayToCopy.length];
examples_not_presenet.explanation: .length is correctly used to determine the size of the copy array
No concrete evidence of the misconception since n is representing the length of the arrays

Arrays_Grow.short_definition: Learners believe that the length of an array is flexible, so they can freely add or remove elements.
Arrays_Grow.why_incorrect: In Processing arrays have a fixed length that is determined when the array is created and cannot be changed afterwards. To store more elements you must create a new array with the desired size and copy the old elements into it.
indicators: Code attempts to write beyond the last valid index of the array
Creating an array of length 0 and then trying to add elements

Trying to use methods or operators that do not exist for arrays in Processing: Students sometimes invent syntax based on intuition, experience with other programming languages, or from examples they’ve seen online. E.g., trying to use add(), append(), or similar methods that do not exist for arrays in Processing.
when_not_a_misconception: Creating a new array with the desired size and copying the old elements into it
Over-allocating an array and tracking the current count separately
Using ArrayList or other dynamic data structures instead of arrays

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Attempting to add elements to an array (c) of length 0
Writing beyond the last valid index

examples_not_presenet.explanation: Correctly creating an array (xPosTemp) with increased size and copying elements
Over-allocating an array and tracking the current count separately

Loops_for_Array_Index_Access.short_definition: Learners tend to believe that a loop is always needed to access an element of an array, even if the index of the respective element is already known.
Loops_for_Array_Index_Access.why_incorrect: Accessing an element of an array does not require a loop when the index of the element is already known. Using a loop in such cases adds unnecessary complexity and inefficiency to the code. Instead, the element can be accessed directly using its index.
indicators: Using a loop to access an element of an array with a known index
if statements inside loops that check for a specific index to access an element
when_not_a_misconception: Using loops to access elements of an array when the indices are not known in advance.

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Using a loop to access the element at known index declared in variable z (3)
Using a loop to access the element at fixed known index (3)

examples_not_presenet.explanation: Directly accessing the element at known index (3) without a loop

One_Loop_per_Array.short_definition: Learners think that each array must be iterated in its own separate loop, even when arrays are structurally aligned (i.e., same length) and logically connected. This leads to code duplication and hides the fact that the data in the arrays is conceptually linked at corresponding indices.
One_Loop_per_Array.why_incorrect: While separate loops are not syntactically wrong, they introduce unnecessary redundancy and obscure the structural relationship between arrays. They also make the code longer and harder to maintain, increase the likelihood of mistakes (e.g. mismatched loop lengths or inconsistent logic) and they reduce clarity by hiding that the index represents the same conceptual entity (e.g. ball, player etc.) across multiple arrays. Using one loop for parallel arrays reveals this connection and improves code quality.
indicators: Multiple independent loops to iterate over related arrays, even when these arrays are of the same length and should be processed together
when_not_a_misconception: Using separate loops for arrays of different lengths
Processing logic between loops is fundamentally different

examples_misconception_presenet.explanation: Using separate loops to initialize related arrays position and speed
Using separate loops to initialize and draw the same array vec

examples_not_presenet.explanation: Using a single loop to initialize related arrays position and speed
